title: Present Active Indicative
description: The present tense of λύω and the verb endings that show the subject.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: The Greek verb shows its subject by its ending. λύω means I loose; λύομεν, we loose. There is no separate word for "I" or "we" unless it is stressed. The present tense means both "I loose" and "I am loosing".

blocks.caption: Present active indicative of λύω
rows: Take off the -ω of the first person to find the present stem (λυ-), then add the endings -ω, -εις, -ει, -ομεν, -ετε, -ουσι(ν). Every verb of this lesson goes the same way: βλέπω, βλέπεις, βλέπει …

blocks.caption: Two kinds of "you"
blocks.html: Greek keeps singular and plural "you" apart. The course writes them as you (sg.) and you (pl.); older English used thou and ye, and the typed answers accept those too.

blocks.caption: Verb accent
blocks.html: The accent of a verb goes as far back from the end as the length of the ultima allows: λύομεν, but λύω. This "recessive" accent holds for nearly all verb forms.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: λύουσι and λύουσιν are the same form: the ν (movable ν) is added before a vowel or at the end of a sentence, and the course accepts either.
